title: Wafer Pricing by Node: 2026 vs 2025 Comparison
abstract: Our procurement desk just closed Q2 books, and the node-by-node damage is worse than the headline numbers suggest.
body:
## The Q2 2026 bill nobody wants to sign

I run procurement for a mid-size fabless shop, and I have the Q2 2026 invoices in front of me. As of 2026-05-15, our blended wafer cost across all nodes is up 19.4% versus the same quarter in 2025. That is not a typo. We are 20 weeks into the year and I have already burned through the entire cost-down budget I fought for in December. The foundries know it. My TSMC rep knows it. Every email I send gets a reply within an hour now, which tells you everything about who has leverage.

Let me be blunt: the 2025 pricing environment was a buyer's market for anything above 7nm. We squeezed. We got concessions. That is over. What follows is what I am actually paying, node by node, with the week counts and the dated figures. No analyst deck, no sell-side fantasy. Just the purchase orders.

## 5nm and 4nm: the pain is concentrated here

In Q2 2025 we were paying $16,800 per 300mm wafer for N5 family capacity on a 12-week lead time. As of 2026-05-15, the same wafer is $19,400. That is a 15.5% jump in 52 weeks. For N4, we went from $18,200 to $21,300, a 17.0% increase. The lead time is now 18 weeks, and my foundry partner will not budge below a 24-week rolling forecast commitment.

Here is the part that stings. We are not a whale. We are a 9,000 wafer-per-quarter account. In 2025 that got us a dedicated AE and a modest volume discount. In 2026 it gets us a polite email and a slot in the queue. The AI accelerator crowd is eating the capacity, and they are paying whatever it takes. I have seen quotes for N4 at $23,000 for smaller accounts. We are getting a deal by comparison, which is a sentence I never thought I would write.

## 7nm and 6nm: the quiet squeeze

N7 was supposed to be the workhorse node where we could hide from the bleeding edge. Not anymore. Q2 2025: $9,800 per wafer. Q2 2026: $11,600. That is 18.4% in 52 weeks. N6 went from $10,400 to $12,300, up 18.3%. Lead times stretched from 10 weeks to 16 weeks.

The excuse I get is wafer starts reallocation. The foundries are pushing 7nm-class capacity toward automotive and industrial customers who sign three-year take-or-pay deals. We sign one-year rolling. Guess who gets the short end. I have started telling my design team to think hard about whether that extra 15% performance on N6 is worth the 18% cost premium over N7. Sometimes it is. Often it is not.

## 16nm and 12nm: the last sane neighborhood

If you want a reason not to panic, look here. N16 in Q2 2025 was $5,200 per wafer. Q2 2026 is $5,700. That is 9.6% in 52 weeks. N12 went from $5,900 to $6,500, up 10.2%. Lead times are stable at 8 to 10 weeks. My foundry partners are still willing to talk about volume tiers. This is where I am moving every design that can tolerate the performance hit.

The catch is that everyone else is doing the same thing. I have heard from two peers in the last 6 weeks that 16nm capacity is tightening for Q4 2026 bookings. If you need wafers in the second half, book now. I am not joking. The window is closing faster than the node comparison suggests.

## 28nm and above: boring, cheap, and getting crowded

N28 was $2,900 per wafer in Q2 2025. Q2 2026 is $3,100. That is 6.9% in 52 weeks. N40 and N65 are basically flat, up 3% to 4%. Lead times are 6 to 8 weeks. For PMICs, MCUs, and anything that does not need to be fast, this is still the bargain bin.

But here is the twist. The mature node fabs are not adding capacity. They are converting some 28nm lines to 22nm and 16nm to chase better margins. That means the cheap stuff is getting less cheap by attrition. I have a 28nm PMIC that I used to buy at $2,750 in 2024. Today it is $3,100. In 2027 I expect it to be $3,400. The direction is one way.

## What I am doing about it

First, I am renegotiating every contract that comes up for renewal in the next 12 weeks. The foundries are not offering discounts, but they are offering priority slots for a premium. I am buying priority on two critical N5 parts and eating the cost. Second, I am moving three designs from N6 to N16. The performance loss is 12% to 15%, but the cost saving is 47% per wafer. My product managers hate it. My CFO loves it. Third, I am building a 26-week buffer on the 16nm and 28nm parts because I do not trust the lead time stability.

The macro picture does not help. The Bank of Japan is still fiddling with yield curve control, which means yen volatility is a real line item in my wafer contracts. TSMC is holding the line on pricing and I do not see that changing before Q1 2027. If you are a fabless shop and you have not re-forecasted your 2026 wafer spend in the last 8 weeks, you are already behind. I know because I was behind 4 weeks ago. The numbers above are what it cost to catch up.
